summary:
Paul founded the church in Corinth around AD 50 and stayed a year and a half; this letter comes a few years later, written from Ephesus after troubling reports and a list of questions arrived from the church. Corinth was a wealthy Roman port city, competitive and status-conscious, and its church mirrored the city: gifted, enthusiastic, and quarreling about nearly everything. Paul works through the problems one at a time: rival factions, a sexual scandal, lawsuits between believers, marriage, food offered to idols, disorder in worship, and doubts about resurrection.

One idea drives every answer: "we preach Christ crucified, a stumbling block to Jews and foolishness to Gentiles" (1:23). A crucified Messiah upends every human ranking of wisdom, power, and status, and Paul keeps applying that reversal to whatever the Corinthians are boasting about. Along the way come passages of unusual historical weight. His instructions on the Lord's Supper in chapter 11 are the earliest written account of that meal, set down before any of the gospels. And chapter 13, read at countless weddings, was written for a church tearing itself apart: without love, the most impressive spiritual gifts amount to noise.

The letter builds to chapter 15, Paul's longest argument for the resurrection of the dead, aimed at members who denied the dead would rise (likely influenced by Greek ideas that the body is inferior to the soul). For Paul the stakes are total: "if Christ has not been raised, your faith is futile; you are still in your sins" (15:17). As you read, watch how the cross reshapes each dispute in turn.
